# Founding Fuel: Geopolitics & International Relations — Batch 1 (2015–2021)
## Dense Observation Set

---

## RECURRING ARGUMENTS

**1. China's rise from copycat to innovator is real and accelerating**
FF repeatedly returns to this arc — from imitation to innovation — treating it as a settled trajectory rather than a hypothesis.

"Rather than being a government, regulation, [or] cultural problem, the issue is that there [had been] no need to be innovative. If you [were] well connected in the 1990s, you could get a plot of land for below market price..." — SOURCE: "Shaun Rein on How China Will Become an Innovative Economy" by CKGSB Knowledge (2015-03-16)

"The most striking feature of innovation in China is the sheer quantum of resources that the country invests in R&D. At $162 billion, this is around 2% of GDP... only 30% of the R&D spend is attributable to the government and most of the rest is by business. In India, the ratio is the opposite!" — SOURCE: "The Chinese innovation machine" by Rishikesha T Krishnan (2016-05-25)

"Beijing's technological capabilities are no more based on the imitation of Western technological products. Nor are they based on stealing others' technology and engaging in IPR violations. It would be a grave error to dismiss China as merely a 'near-peer competitor'." — SOURCE: "The US-China war for tech supremacy is splitting the world in two" by G Venkat Raman (2020-10-15)

**2. China's state-directed capitalism is a coherent and effective model**
FF consistently frames China's political-economy as purposeful rather than arbitrary — the government designs markets, rewards winners, and protects strategic sectors.

"The government knows that a state-controlled enterprise will not be able to harness the energy of its entrepreneurs, so it carves out markets for them to play in, provides a cushion of state debt and benign regulations and allows them to build scale rapidly." — SOURCE: "The Uber-Didi deal is more about China than about Uber and Didi" by Haresh Chawla (2016-08-02)

"China has demonstrated again and again that it will not allow foreigners to control its vital assets—and what's more vital than its entire digital ecosystem?" — SOURCE: "The Uber-Didi deal is more about China than about Uber and Didi" by Haresh Chawla (2016-08-02)

"The Chinese authorities subsidized tech entrepreneurs with calls from the State Council to create thousands of tech incubators." — SOURCE: "State Vs Big Tech: The three drivers of Chinese techlash" by G Venkat Raman (2021-09-09)

**3. The US-China rivalry is civilizational, not just commercial, and is restructuring the global order**
From 2019 onward, FF consistently frames the US-China contest as the defining geopolitical fact of the era.

"Today, the Sino-US 'techonomic' war is mostly seen as a race for dominance in AI." — SOURCE: "The US-China war for tech supremacy is splitting the world in two" by G Venkat Raman (2020-10-15)

"We are beginning to see the world dividing in two camps, led by the US and China... Whenever the world is divided into two camps, there is bound to be some kind of a confrontation at some stage." — SOURCE: "How the world has moved in the first quarter of 2021" by Founding Fuel (2021-04-14)

"The cold war between the US and China is on the rise and it will characterise the years of the Biden presidency and beyond. This last quarter laid the foundation for a new hostility in the world which could potentially risk the survival of humankind in the next decade or two." — SOURCE: "How the world has moved in the second quarter of 2021" by Founding Fuel (2021-07-20)

**4. Technology and geopolitics are inseparable — "technology is politics"**
This becomes an explicit FF thesis by 2019-2020.

"Technology is politics" — SOURCE: "Technology is politics" by N S Ramnath (2019-07-03) [article title itself is the argument]

"If the US forces countries to choose between itself and China, some will end up choosing China. The US might end up isolating itself..." — SOURCE: "Technology is politics" by N S Ramnath (2019-07-03), citing Henry Paulson's FT column

"The concept of weaponized interdependence gained currency after two US political scientists, Henry Farrell and Abraham Newman, coined and popularised the idea. They argued that the distribution of power in the international economic order rests on control over its critical nodes: financial communications, supply chains, and the internet." — SOURCE: "The US-China war for tech supremacy is splitting the world in two" by G Venkat Raman (2020-10-15)

**5. The "Splinternet" — fragmentation of the global internet — is underway**
FF treats this as an emergent structural reality, not a hypothetical.

"'I do think there is a global tendency towards fragmenting the internet much more than it has been fragmented in the past,' Daphne Keller, director of the program on platform regulation at Stanford University's Cyber Policy Center, told CNN Business." — SOURCE: "FF Daily #309: Splinternet and the new rules of the game" by Founding Fuel (2021-02-26)

"Suppose there is no resolution of the US-China dispute, the world is likely to stare at a possibility where the internet world will be divided into two worlds. Some refer to this as 'one world, two systems'." — SOURCE: "The US-China war for tech supremacy is splitting the world in two" by G Venkat Raman (2020-10-15)

**6. India should be a confident, globally engaged player — not protectionist or fearful**
This normative argument appears repeatedly, often implicitly in contrast to what FF observes India actually doing.

"A confident India, which is already a lower middle-income country, and which needs to avoid the middle-income trap, should not be afraid to engage with the world, for trade, for investment, for ideas, for innovation. Embracing economic isolation at this turning point in the global system will be a strategic mistake." — SOURCE: "WFH Daily #116: Why India should bat for globalisation now" by Founding Fuel (2020-07-17), citing Kelkar, Mashelkar, Rajadhyaksha

"It's important for India to understand this rivalry, so it can tweak its own relationship with China, guided by facts, reasoning and a healthy dose of pragmatism, rather than by pride or fear, especially during these emotionally charged times." — SOURCE: "The US-China war for tech supremacy is splitting the world in two" by G Venkat Raman (2020-10-15)

---

## FF'S INDIA-SPECIFIC ANGLE

**India as aspirational comparison to China — but consistently behind**
The India-China comparison is a persistent undercurrent. FF's Indian readers are implicitly asked to measure India against China's trajectory.

"Just as a reference point, R&D spending in India has never crossed 1% of GDP, and is generally around 0.8-0.9%... In India, the ratio is the opposite [of China's, where business does most R&D]!" — SOURCE: "The Chinese innovation machine" by Rishikesha T Krishnan (2016-05-25)

"Almost every business school dean we met [in China] mentioned that the Indian economy would be growing faster than the Chinese economy this year." — SOURCE: "The dragon mellows" by Rishikesha T Krishnan (2015-11-04)

The psychological moment: Chinese academics who previously ignored India suddenly sought meetings with Indian business school faculty when India's GDP growth overtook China's. — SOURCE: "The dragon mellows" by Rishikesha T Krishnan (2015-11-04)

**India as potential democracy counterweight to China's model — but not yet seizing that role**
"India, which already has examples of digital public infrastructure such as Aadhaar and UPI, and societal platforms such as Ek Step, can lend its voice to make AI a global public good." — SOURCE: "AI as a global public good, a digitised world, and why philosophy matters" by N S Ramnath (2019-02-19)

**India's Afghanistan dilemma — strategic interest vs. principled position**
"Exiting Afghanistan totally does not suit India's geopolitical interests either... there is a palpable fear it can be used as a base to launch terror strikes against India." — SOURCE: "FF Daily #425: The Afghan front" by Founding Fuel (2021-07-17)

The report notes India was late to engage the Taliban while Russia, China, and Iran had already opened channels. "India declined as a matter of principle." — SOURCE: "FF Daily #425: The Afghan front" by Founding Fuel (2021-07-17)

**India's vulnerability to Chinese tech penetration**
"Today Chinese smartphones and apps are ubiquitous in India and in the process they have built a successful playbook for launching products to Indian consumers... With that kind of access and control on data, Chinese AI will have the most information to train the AI algorithms with. In such a scenario, India will have to depend on the Chinese to get insights into healthcare trends and treatments." — SOURCE: "Algorithmic War is upon us" by Founding Fuel (2019-08-04)

**India's political volatility in the context of geopolitics**
Obama quoting Manmohan Singh: "'In uncertain times, Mr. President,' the prime minister said, 'the call of religious and ethnic solidarity can be intoxicating. And it's not so hard for politicians to exploit that, in India or anywhere else.'" — SOURCE: "FF Daily #233: When Barack Obama met Manmohan Singh" by Founding Fuel (2020-11-19)

**India-Pakistan as colonial legacy problem**
"It was only a little while ago that well known journalist and television anchor Rajdeep Sardesai posted a picture on his Twitter handle of MS Dhoni holding the Pakistani skipper Sarfraz Ahmed's baby. What else needs to be said?... They were the ones who first sowed the seeds of discord among the 'brown natives'." — SOURCE: "India versus Pakistan is not cricket, but war" by Charles Assisi (2017-06-18)

**The Indian Army at Ladakh — costs of confronting China**
Sandeep Unnithan's reportage quoted: "It costs the Indian Army Rs 5 crore a day to maintain a brigade of troops, over 3,000 soldiers, on the Siachen glacier." — SOURCE: "WFH Daily #189: The Indian Army in Ladakh" by Founding Fuel (2020-09-28)

**India as central to US strategy on China**
"The US has come to view India as central to how it will deal with China in the Indo-Pacific region." — SOURCE: "How the world has moved in the first quarter of 2021" by Founding Fuel (2021-04-14)

---

## FRAMEWORKS, THINKERS, MENTAL MODELS

**Kishore Mahbubani — Asian century, Western decline**
His framing that "For 1,800 of the past 2,000 years, the world's two largest economies have always been [China and India]. The last 200 years have been a major historical aberration." is cited approvingly. — SOURCE: "The West in an era of Asian dominance" by CKGSB Knowledge (2018-12-12)

He also provides the Fukuyama critique: "Fukuyama's essay did a lot of brain damage to the West. He put the West to sleep precisely at the moment when China and India were waking up." — SOURCE: "The West in an era of Asian dominance" by CKGSB Knowledge (2018-12-12)

**Henry Paulson — inside-track China knowledge**
Used twice: first for his book *Dealing with China* as a source of ground-level understanding of Chinese leadership; then cited in 2019 for his FT column warning about US isolation if it forces countries to choose sides on Huawei. — SOURCE: "Understanding China: Insights from Henry Paulson's book" by Rishikesha T Krishnan (2015-07-11); "Technology is politics" by N S Ramnath (2019-07-03)

**Kai-Fu Lee — China as "Saudi Arabia of data"**
Lee's "age of implementation" framing is adopted: "China's transformation from being a copycat economy to an innovation economy has led to China's emergence as the 'Saudi Arabia of data' in an age in which data is the new oil." — SOURCE: "Should the world be worried about Chinese tech?" by G Venkat Raman (2020-10-19)

**Lee Kuan Yew — governance, Singapore model, multilateral approach to extremism**
Cited at his death anniversary for leadership lessons, and later for insights on Islamist terrorism and the Pakistan-terror nexus. "We should learn to live with the Pakistan-terror nexus for a long time. My fear is Pakistan may well get worse." — SOURCE: "Lee Kuan Yew: A leadership style that got results" by Founding Fuel (2016-03-23); "FF Daily #471: Lee Kuan Yew on reining extremism" by Founding Fuel (2021-09-10)

**Henry Farrell & Abraham Newman — "Weaponized interdependence"**
"The distribution of power in the international economic order rests on control over its critical nodes: financial communications, supply chains, and the internet." — SOURCE: "The US-China war for tech supremacy is splitting the world in two" by G Venkat Raman (2020-10-15)

**Steve Blank / Lean Startup — applied to China's entrepreneurial ecosystem**
Blank's observation that "sea turtles" (returning Chinese students) act as "physical VPNs" to transfer Silicon Valley knowledge to China is a vivid metaphor FF found worth featuring. — SOURCE: "Red Star Rising: A Q&A With Steve Blank" by CKGSB Knowledge (2015-08-06)

**Sundeep Waslekar / Strategic Foresight Group — FF's recurring geopolitics guide**
From late 2020, Waslekar becomes FF's quarterly interpreter of global developments. His framing of "world dividing into two camps" and the nuclear arms race as the true existential crisis (bigger than Covid or climate) shapes FF's geopolitical coverage. — SOURCE: "How the world has moved in the first quarter of 2021" by Founding Fuel (2021-04-14); "How the world has moved in the second quarter of 2021" by Founding Fuel (2021-07-20)

**Will & Ariel Durant — history as recurring pattern**
Used to contextualize the India-Pakistan rivalry and technology disruption. "Everything repeats itself. Over. And over. Again." — SOURCE: "Life is unfair. Deal with it" by Charles Assisi (2017-07-10)

**"Brussels Effect" — EU regulation as de facto global standard**
"More than 120 countries are taking inspiration from GDPR in framing their own rules for the technology sector." — SOURCE: "State Vs Big Tech: The Brussels Effect" by G Venkat Raman (2021-09-13)

**"Glocalization" — global strategy with local adaptation**
The Disney Shanghai case ("Authentically Disney, Distinctly Chinese") becomes a lens for how MNCs must operate in China and by extension in India. — SOURCE: "Shanghai Disney's Chinese track and fighting obesity with taxes" by Rajesh Srivastava (2016-10-24)

**Three-stage innovation model for Chinese companies** (Yip & McKern)
Stage 1: "fit for purpose" products for local market. Stage 2: up to world standards. Stage 3: global leadership. — SOURCE: "The Chinese innovation machine" by Rishikesha T Krishnan (2016-05-25)

---

## WHAT FF IS SKEPTICAL OF / PUSHES BACK AGAINST

**Western dismissal of China's innovation capacity**
"It would be wrong to underestimate China as Joe Biden did." — SOURCE: "Shaun Rein on How China Will Become an Innovative Economy" by CKGSB Knowledge (2015-03-16)

FF treats Biden's "can you name one innovative product from China?" challenge as a straw man worth demolishing — and returns to this theme across several years.

# Founding Fuel: Geopolitics & International Relations — Batch 2 (2021-11-24 to 2024-09-17)

## Dense Observations with Sources

---

## RECURRING ARGUMENTS FF MAKES

**1. The world is fragmenting into blocs — but not cleanly**

"The world as we knew it after the 1991 fall of the Soviet Union has disappeared" — SOURCE: "Briefing 1: How a fragmented world will impact trade & corporate strategy" by Vivek Y. Kelkar (2024-09-17)

"Geopolitics has trumped geoeconomics" — SOURCE: "The World in 2022: Events that shaped our world" by Founding Fuel (2022-12-26), via Niranjan Rajadhyaksha

Friend-shoring "will not fracture the global system into exclusive trading zones, but it will create barriers in critical industries such as semiconductors, biotechnology, artificial intelligence, green mobility and new forms of energy" — SOURCE: "The World in 2022: Events that shaped our world" (2022-12-26)

"There's one bloc that's US-inclined, another led by China & Russia, and a likely third that would ideally like to straddle these two blocs with countries like India, Vietnam and Brazil" — SOURCE: "Briefing 1: How a fragmented world will impact trade & corporate strategy" (2024-09-17)

**2. Nuclear risk is real and underappreciated**

"Humanity was one miscalculation away from nuclear annihilation" (quoting Guterres) — SOURCE: "Nuclear War: A 100 seconds to midnight" by Sundeep Waslekar (2022-11-10)

"The Doomsday Clock at 90 seconds to midnight" — SOURCE: "Is the world increasingly becoming a dangerous place to live?" by Sundeep Waslekar (2023-12-11)

"The existential threat to human civilization stems from the growing nexus between artificial intelligence, nuclear weapons, and biotechnology" — SOURCE: "Is the world increasingly becoming a dangerous place to live?" (2023-12-11)

**3. US hegemony is declining but not collapsed; China has risen but has real limits**

"Neither fits into the framework of an absolute hegemon" — SOURCE: "The future of hegemony: Asymmetric cooperation" by Vivek Y. Kelkar (2024-05-07)

"The US' power to induce action and punish has not amounted to much in recent decades. Neither sanctions over Russia, nor its recent military actions in Afghanistan and Iraq have been wholly successful" — SOURCE: "The future of hegemony: Asymmetric cooperation" (2024-05-07)

"The US is not in strategic retreat and a rising China does not have the capability to dominate this space for the foreseeable future" — SOURCE: "Is the US in strategic retreat in the Indian Ocean region?" by Kanti Prasad Bajpai (2023-12-18)

**4. Russia punches far above its weight**

"Russia is now more influential on global affairs than at any time since the 1970s" — SOURCE: "FF Life: The Best Stories of 2021" (2022-02-12), summarizing "From Russia with Love" by Samuel Pepys (2021-12-15)

"Where the U.S. and China pour billions to buy a little goodwill and influence, Russia walks in and takes a controlling interest at virtually no cost. Moscow punching far above its weight may well turn out to be the biggest geopolitical surprise of the 21st Century" — SOURCE: "From Russia with Love" by Samuel Pepys (2021-12-15)

"Its gross domestic product—smaller than that of Guangdong or New York state—is struggling to grow" — SOURCE: "From Russia with Love" by Samuel Pepys (2021-12-15)

**5. China uses deception, constructed narratives, and false victimhood as tools of foreign policy**

"The CPC's great skill in constructing false narratives, including its playing victim of Western imperialism as a way of extracting concessions... China's art of getting its detractors to apologize for slights real and imagined is probably worth a book in itself" — SOURCE: "The practice of Chinese foreign policy" by Jabin T. Jacob (2023-03-06)

"Deception is often seen as another fine art in the practice of Chinese foreign policy" — SOURCE: "The practice of Chinese foreign policy" (2023-03-06)

"The West—the US and the Europeans—for their greed, willful blindness and hypocrisy in policies towards China ignoring India's experiences with China and its warnings until quite recently" — SOURCE: "The practice of Chinese foreign policy" (2023-03-06)

**6. The US-China tech war has systemic global consequences, not just bilateral ones**

"The 'foreign product rule' is a pretty draconian measure that grants US export controls greater extraterritorial reach" — SOURCE: "US-China Tech war: The US is weaponizing its global influence" by G Venkat Raman (2022-12-01)

"It might seem that only Chinese firms will be majorly hit... But this is going to have implications for American firms, non-American and non-Chinese firms as well" — SOURCE: "The best stories of 2022" (2022-12-23), quoting Venkat Raman

"Whoever owns the standards, owns the market" — SOURCE: "US-China Tech war: The US is weaponizing its global influence" (2022-12-01)

**7. Multilateralism is under severe strain; global governance institutions are failing**

"In August the nuclear non-proliferation review conference failed. In December, the test ban treaty collapsed" — SOURCE: "Is the world increasingly becoming a dangerous place to live?" (2023-12-11)

"Those who die instantly will be fortunate. The rest of us will suffer from radiation, environmental impact, blackout of sunrays, disease of flora and fauna, and a slow and torturous death" — SOURCE: "Nuclear War: A 100 seconds to midnight" (2022-11-10)

## INDIA-SPECIFIC ANGLE

**India's strategic ambiguity as deliberate policy (celebrated but also scrutinized)**

"If there is a China-India conflict of a serious nature, Russia will try to play peacemaker. It cannot afford to lose either China (a big market for agriculture) or India (for its defence equipment). And New Delhi expects it. Despite all our bravado, we know we are weak vis-a-[vis China]" — SOURCE: "FF Insights #608: The Munger Way" (2022-03-14), summarizing the Russia-Ukraine masterclass

"India sides with the US [on geopolitics]; when it comes to climate politics India sides with China" — SOURCE: "Masterclass: The World in 2022" by Founding Fuel (2021-12-20)

"The clear preference for more trade between geopolitical allies could also mean persistent pressure on India to choose between the opposing camps, rather than occupy the middle ground as it quite rightly has in the case of Russian oil right now" — SOURCE: "The World in 2022: Events that shaped our world" (2022-12-26)

**India and China: LAC diplomacy and the limits of negotiation**

Detailed account of how India's 1993 Border Peace and Tranquillity Agreement (BPTA) was negotiated — accepted a formulation on the LAC that "did not conclusively reject the Chinese version of the LAC" because the alternative "might have been a continued state of close confrontation all along the LAC at a time when India was battling Pakistan-sponsored terrorism in both Punjab and Jammu and Kashmir" — SOURCE: "India's negotiations with China: The boundary question" by Founding Fuel (2022-09-30)

"The idea of the LAC itself was a Chinese creation" — SOURCE: "India's negotiations with China: The boundary question" (2022-09-30)

**India's 'Neighbourhood First' policy seen as having failed**

"India has made inadequate investments in political relationships and economic integration with neighbours in the past decade" — SOURCE: "Fire in the 'hood" by Dinesh Narayanan (2024-09-06)

"The neighbourhood has suffered relative neglect with the pursuit of a high global profile" (quoting former foreign secretary Shyam Saran) — SOURCE: "Fire in the 'hood" (2024-09-06)

India's support for Sheikh Hasina was "so unequivocal that it looked away as she brutally cracked down on the opposition" — SOURCE: "Fire in the 'hood" (2024-09-06)

**India as potential Global South leader — with caveats**

"Indian diplomats consulted over 120 governments before the G20 summit. They discovered huge resentment among developing countries, especially in Africa, against the West... these same developing countries were also increasingly sceptical about China" — SOURCE: "Is India too late to the Global South party?" by Pramit Pal Chaudhuri (2023-12-23)

"India avoids calling itself a Global South leader. Modi instead talks about a 'new multilateralism'" — SOURCE: "Is India too late to the Global South party?" (2023-12-23)

"What is not clear is whether India has the wherewithal to take on that mantle" — SOURCE: "Is India too late to the Global South party?" (2023-12-23)

**India and China in the Indian Ocean: US-India complementarity**

"A combination of American and Indian naval and air power would be devastating to Chinese ships and aircraft in Djibouti, Gwadar (if Pakistan allows use of Gwadar as a military facility—which is not a given), Hambantota, and Kyaukpyu" — SOURCE: "Is the US in strategic retreat in the Indian Ocean region?" by Kanti Prasad Bajpai (2023-12-18)

**India must boost tech prowess and voice in international fora**

"India must boost its tech prowess and voice in international fora" — SOURCE: "US-China Tech war: The US is weaponizing its global influence" (2022-12-01)

**India-China 1962 shadow**

"If India and China stood together for twenty years, 'no one would be able to make us go on different paths'" (Mao to Radhakrishnan, recalled by Natwar Singh). "Twenty years were reduced to five, when China attacked India in 1962" — SOURCE: "FF Insights #648: 'If India and China stood together…'" by Founding Fuel (2022-06-04)

## FRAMEWORKS, THINKERS, MENTAL MODELS

**Sundeep Waslekar / Strategic Foresight Group** — appears in virtually every geopolitics masterclass. His framing of the Doomsday Clock, nuclear risk, Middle East mediation, and Russia's outsized influence recurs across articles from 2021 through 2024. SOURCE: Multiple articles.

**Realist international relations paradigm** — explicitly invoked: "New contours are being drawn across global economic and power systems... each based in realist international relations paradigms" — SOURCE: "The future of hegemony: Asymmetric cooperation" (2024-05-07)

**Robert Keohane's hegemony theory (1984)** — "as the US became less preponderant in material resources, its hegemonic powers would wane... 'The subjective elements of American hegemony have been eroded'" — SOURCE: "The future of hegemony: Asymmetric cooperation" (2024-05-07)

**Doomsday Clock / Bulletin of Atomic Scientists** — used repeatedly as a framework for nuclear risk communication. SOURCE: "Nuclear War: A 100 seconds to midnight" (2022-11-10); "Is the world increasingly becoming a dangerous place to live?" (2023-12-11)

**"The decade of the 20s will resemble the decade of the 1920s"** — Waslekar's historical analogy: "Mussolini and Hitler became popular. So, democracies will again bring nationalist forces to power like it did a 100 years ago" — SOURCE: "Masterclass: The World in 2024" (2024-02-06)

**Clayton-Maggiori-Schreger framework (2023)** — "geopolitical power arises from the ability of a country to consolidate disparate threats across multiple economic domains" — SOURCE: "The future of hegemony: Asymmetric cooperation" (2024-05-07)

**"Finnish Model" as a counterfactual for Ukraine** — what Ukraine could have been had it declared neutrality; Finland "slowly but decidedly moved westward" while nominally neutral — SOURCE: "FF Insights #591: Putin versus Ukraine" (2022-02-19)

**"Japanification" of China** — JP Morgan analysts' framework: "protracted period of 'deflation, economic sluggishness, decline in the property market and financial stress'" — SOURCE: "China's economic shift: Politics trumps growth" by G Venkat Raman (2023-09-25)

**Belt and Road Initiative (BRI)** — appears repeatedly as China's geo-economic instrument, now showing signs of strain. "BRI projects were often uncoordinated. Economic gains to the recipient nations were opaquely defined... left quite a few nations with extensive and out-of-control debt" — SOURCE: "Is Africa swapping out Europe for China?" by Vivek Y. Kelkar (2023-12-20)

**"Striving for Achievement" (SFA) vs "lying low" policy shift in China** — Xi switched policies post-2008; cited as structural cause of US-China deterioration — SOURCE: "Does the current US-China detente signal a thawing of relations?" by G Venkat Raman (2023-12-15)

**Mutually Assured Destruction (MAD) — economic version** — "Neither of them wants an economic MAD (mutually assured destruction)" re US-China — SOURCE: "Does the current US-China detente signal a thawing of relations?" (2023-12-15)

# Founding Fuel: Geopolitics & International Relations — Batch 3 (Sept 2024–March 2026)

## Dense Observational Notes

---

### I. RECURRING ARGUMENTS FF MAKES

**1. The securitization of everything economic**
The most persistent refrain across this entire batch is that economic flows—goods, capital, data, technology, people—have been refracted through a national security prism, destroying the old separation between security competition and business.
- "Nearly everything, especially economic flows, have been securitised — flows of goods, capital, people, data and especially technology — are being refracted by the political class, the strategic class and regulatory class in Washington through the prism of national security rather than public good." — SOURCE: "Masterclass: Geopolitics and Global Trade - How It Impacts India" by Founding Fuel (2024-09-17)
- "The interdependence that powered globalisation is now being weaponised." — SOURCE: "The New Perimeter of National Security" by G Venkat Raman (2025-12-08)

**2. The US is strategically incoherent—wanting outcomes without committing instruments**
FF returns again and again to the gap between US ambitions and US willingness to commit trade policy, alliances, or industrial strategy.
- "The US might find it no longer has the leverage it once did to shape Asian trade and economics... The US remains unwilling to commit to trade policy as a broad foreign policy tool. ### II. FF'S INDIA-SPECIFIC ANGLE

**India's defining dilemma: strategic autonomy is structural, not rhetorical**
FF's most distinctive India angle is that India's famous "strategic autonomy" doctrine is being tested not by ideology but by structural dependencies—energy, trade, technology, and geography.
- "The very region that enables India's strategic autonomy is also the one most capable of constraining it when instability erupts." — SOURCE: "The US–Israel War on Iran: The Risks to India's Strategic Hedging" by Vivek Y. Kelkar (2026-03-04)
- "Autonomy today is less about refusal and more about calibration. India has bought time—but at the cost of signalling a willingness to align with Washington's priorities." — SOURCE: "India's Trade Deals and the New Meaning of Strategic Autonomy" by Vivek Y. Kelkar (2026-02-09)
- "Strategic autonomy, in this context, is the capacity to retain economic and diplomatic choices." — SOURCE: "Trade Is the New Geopolitics—and India Must Learn to Play It" by Vivek Y. Kelkar (2026-01-19)

**India as a "rule-shaper" manqué—aspiring but not yet arriving**

- "The problem with Indian AI policy is, it's made by MeitY and Niti Aayog... I don't know how much the National Security Council is involved." — Waslekar, quoted in SOURCE: "India's AI Gambit" by Founding Fuel (2025-07-10)
